cards.q: What is the moment of inertia of a body, and what is it for a point mass?
cards.a: A measure of how hard it is to change the body's rotational motion. For a point mass m\displaystyle mm at distance r\displaystyle rr from the axis, I=mr2\displaystyle I = mr^{2}I=mr2; for an extended object, I=Σmr2\displaystyle I = \Sigma mr^{2}I=Σmr2. Unit: kg m2\displaystyle \text{kg m}^{2}kg m2.

cards.q: What two things determine the moment of inertia of a rotating object?
cards.a: Its mass, and how that mass is distributed about the axis of rotation. Mass further from the axis gives a larger moment of inertia.

cards.q: Calculate the moment of inertia of a 2.0 kg point mass rotating 0.50 m from an axis.
cards.a: 0.50 kg m2\displaystyle 0.50\ \text{kg m}^{2}0.50 kg m2
steps: I=mr2=2.0×0.502\displaystyle I = mr^{2} = 2.0 \times 0.50^{2}I=mr2=2.0×0.502
I=0.50 kg m2\displaystyle I = 0.50\ \text{kg m}^{2}I=0.50 kg m2

cards.q: Write the equation for rotational kinetic energy.
cards.a: Ek=12Iω2\displaystyle E_{k} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}Ek​=21​Iω2

cards.q: A flywheel of moment of inertia 0.80 kg m2\displaystyle 0.80\ \text{kg m}^{2}0.80 kg m2 rotates at 50 rad s−1\displaystyle 50\ \text{rad s}^{-1}50 rad s−1. Calculate its rotational kinetic energy.
cards.a: 1.0×103 J\displaystyle 1.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J}1.0×103 J
steps: Ek=12Iω2=12×0.80×502\displaystyle E_{k} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.80 \times 50^{2}Ek​=21​Iω2=21​×0.80×502
Ek=1.0×103 J\displaystyle E_{k} = 1.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J}Ek​=1.0×103 J

cards.q: What factors affect how much energy a flywheel can store?
cards.a: Its moment of inertia, which depends on its mass and on having that mass far from the axis (a heavy rim), and its angular speed. Energy depends on ω2\displaystyle \omega^{2}ω2, so speed matters most; the top speed is limited by the strength of the material.

cards.q: Give two uses of flywheels.
cards.a: Smoothing the torque and speed of an engine, whose power comes in pulses. Storing energy, for example energy recovered from braking in a vehicle, or to deliver a burst of energy in a machine such as a press.

cards.q: Define angular acceleration, and state its unit.
cards.a: The rate of change of angular velocity: α=ΔωΔt\displaystyle \alpha = \frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}α=ΔtΔω​. Unit: rad s−2\displaystyle \text{rad s}^{-2}rad s−2.

cards.q: State the rotational quantities that correspond to displacement, velocity, acceleration, mass, force and momentum.
cards.a: Displacement → angular displacement θ\displaystyle \thetaθ. Velocity → angular velocity ω\displaystyle \omegaω. Acceleration → angular acceleration α\displaystyle \alphaα. Mass → moment of inertia I\displaystyle II. Force → torque T\displaystyle TT. Momentum → angular momentum Iω\displaystyle I\omegaIω.
cards.why: Every equation of linear motion has a rotational twin made with these swaps.

cards.q: Write the four equations for uniform angular acceleration.
cards.a: ω2=ω1+αt\displaystyle \omega_{2} = \omega_{1} + \alpha tω2​=ω1​+αt; θ=(ω1+ω2)t2\displaystyle \theta = \frac{(\omega_{1} + \omega_{2})t}{2}θ=2(ω1​+ω2​)t​; θ=ω1t+12αt2\displaystyle \theta = \omega_{1}t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^{2}θ=ω1​t+21​αt2; ω22=ω12+2αθ\displaystyle \omega_{2}^{2} = \omega_{1}^{2} + 2\alpha\thetaω22​=ω12​+2αθ.

cards.q: A flywheel starts from rest with an angular acceleration of 4.0 rad s−2\displaystyle 4.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}4.0 rad s−2. Calculate its angular speed after 5.0 s.
cards.a: 20 rad s−1\displaystyle 20\ \text{rad s}^{-1}20 rad s−1
steps: ω2=ω1+αt=0+4.0×5.0\displaystyle \omega_{2} = \omega_{1} + \alpha t = 0 + 4.0 \times 5.0ω2​=ω1​+αt=0+4.0×5.0
ω2=20 rad s−1\displaystyle \omega_{2} = 20\ \text{rad s}^{-1}ω2​=20 rad s−1

cards.q: A flywheel starts from rest with an angular acceleration of 4.0 rad s−2\displaystyle 4.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}4.0 rad s−2. Calculate the angle it turns through in 5.0 s.
cards.a: 50 rad (about 8 revolutions)
cards.why: Divide by 2π\displaystyle 2\pi2π to convert radians to revolutions.
steps: θ=ω1t+12αt2=0+12×4.0×5.02\displaystyle \theta = \omega_{1}t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^{2} = 0 + \frac{1}{2} \times 4.0 \times 5.0^{2}θ=ω1​t+21​αt2=0+21​×4.0×5.02
θ=50 rad\displaystyle \theta = 50\ \text{rad}θ=50 rad

cards.q: What do the gradient of an angular velocity–time graph, and the area under it, represent?
cards.a: The gradient is the angular acceleration. The area under the graph is the angular displacement.

cards.q: Write the two equations for torque.
cards.a: T=Fr\displaystyle T = FrT=Fr, where r\displaystyle rr is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force, and T=Iα\displaystyle T = I\alphaT=Iα.
cards.why: T=Iα\displaystyle T = I\alphaT=Iα is the rotational form of F=ma\displaystyle F = maF=ma.

cards.q: A resultant torque of 6.0 N m acts on a wheel of moment of inertia 1.5 kg m2\displaystyle 1.5\ \text{kg m}^{2}1.5 kg m2. Calculate its angular acceleration.
cards.a: 4.0 rad s−2\displaystyle 4.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}4.0 rad s−2
steps: α=TI=6.01.5\displaystyle \alpha = \frac{T}{I} = \frac{6.0}{1.5}α=IT​=1.56.0​
α=4.0 rad s−2\displaystyle \alpha = 4.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}α=4.0 rad s−2

cards.q: A motor applies a torque of 10 N m to a rotor of moment of inertia 4.0 kg m2\displaystyle 4.0\ \text{kg m}^{2}4.0 kg m2. A frictional torque of 2.0 N m opposes the motion. Calculate the angular acceleration.
cards.a: 2.0 rad s−2\displaystyle 2.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}2.0 rad s−2
cards.why: Frictional torque always has to be taken off the applied torque in rotating machinery.
steps: Resultant torque: 10−2.0=8.0 N m\displaystyle 10 - 2.0 = 8.0\ \text{N m}10−2.0=8.0 N m.
α=TI=8.04.0\displaystyle \alpha = \frac{T}{I} = \frac{8.0}{4.0}α=IT​=4.08.0​
α=2.0 rad s−2\displaystyle \alpha = 2.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}α=2.0 rad s−2

cards.q: Define angular momentum, and state its unit.
cards.a: The product of the moment of inertia and the angular velocity: Iω\displaystyle I\omegaIω. Unit: kg m2 s−1\displaystyle \text{kg m}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-1}kg m2 s−1 (or N m s).

cards.q: State the principle of conservation of angular momentum.
cards.a: The total angular momentum of a system stays constant, provided no external torque acts on it.

cards.q: Explain why a spinning ice skater turns faster when she pulls her arms in.
cards.a: Her moment of inertia falls, so her angular velocity must rise.
marks: No external torque acts, so her angular momentum Iω\displaystyle I\omegaIω is conserved.
Pulling her arms in brings mass closer to the axis, which reduces her moment of inertia.
For Iω\displaystyle I\omegaIω to stay the same, her angular velocity must increase.

cards.q: A skater spins at 2.0 rad s−1\displaystyle 2.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}2.0 rad s−1 with a moment of inertia of 4.0 kg m2\displaystyle 4.0\ \text{kg m}^{2}4.0 kg m2. She pulls in her arms, reducing it to 1.6 kg m2\displaystyle 1.6\ \text{kg m}^{2}1.6 kg m2. Calculate her new angular speed.
cards.a: 5.0 rad s−1\displaystyle 5.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}5.0 rad s−1
steps: Angular momentum is conserved: I1ω1=I2ω2\displaystyle I_{1}\omega_{1} = I_{2}\omega_{2}I1​ω1​=I2​ω2​.
4.0×2.0=1.6×ω2\displaystyle 4.0 \times 2.0 = 1.6 \times \omega_{2}4.0×2.0=1.6×ω2​
ω2=5.0 rad s−1\displaystyle \omega_{2} = 5.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}ω2​=5.0 rad s−1

cards.q: When a skater pulls in her arms, her angular momentum is conserved. What happens to her rotational kinetic energy, and where does the change come from?
cards.a: It increases. She does work pulling her arms inwards against the tendency of the mass to move outwards.
cards.why: Ek=12Iω2\displaystyle E_{k} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}Ek​=21​Iω2: with Iω\displaystyle I\omegaIω fixed, a larger ω\displaystyle \omegaω means more energy.

cards.q: A constant torque of 3.0 N m acts for 4.0 s on a wheel of moment of inertia 2.0 kg m2\displaystyle 2.0\ \text{kg m}^{2}2.0 kg m2, initially at rest. Calculate its final angular speed.
cards.a: 6.0 rad s−1\displaystyle 6.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}6.0 rad s−1
steps: Angular impulse = change in angular momentum: TΔt=Δ(Iω)\displaystyle T\Delta t = \Delta(I\omega)TΔt=Δ(Iω).
3.0×4.0=2.0×ω\displaystyle 3.0 \times 4.0 = 2.0 \times \omega3.0×4.0=2.0×ω
ω=6.0 rad s−1\displaystyle \omega = 6.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}ω=6.0 rad s−1

cards.q: Write the equations for the work done by a torque and for the power it delivers.
cards.a: W=Tθ\displaystyle W = T\thetaW=Tθ and P=Tω\displaystyle P = T\omegaP=Tω

cards.q: A motor delivers a torque of 20 N m at an angular speed of 150 rad s−1\displaystyle 150\ \text{rad s}^{-1}150 rad s−1. Calculate its output power.
cards.a: 3.0×103 W\displaystyle 3.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{W}3.0×103 W
steps: P=Tω=20×150\displaystyle P = T\omega = 20 \times 150P=Tω=20×150
P=3.0×103 W\displaystyle P = 3.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{W}P=3.0×103 W

cards.q: State the first law of thermodynamics as an equation, and say what each term means.
cards.a: Q=ΔU+W\displaystyle Q = \Delta U + WQ=ΔU+W: Q\displaystyle QQ is the energy transferred to the system by heating, ΔU\displaystyle \Delta UΔU the increase in its internal energy, and W\displaystyle WW the work done by the system.

cards.q: A gas is supplied with 500 J of energy by heating and does 200 J of work as it expands. Calculate the change in its internal energy.
cards.a: +300 J
steps: ΔU=Q−W=500−200\displaystyle \Delta U = Q - W = 500 - 200ΔU=Q−W=500−200
ΔU=+300 J\displaystyle \Delta U = +300\ \text{J}ΔU=+300 J: the internal energy increases.

cards.q: What is an isothermal change, and what does the first law say about it for an ideal gas?
cards.a: A change at constant temperature: pV=constant\displaystyle pV = \text{constant}pV=constant. The internal energy does not change, so Q=W\displaystyle Q = WQ=W: all the energy supplied by heating is used to do work.

cards.q: What is an adiabatic change, and what does the first law say about it?
cards.a: A change in which no energy is transferred by heating: Q=0\displaystyle Q = 0Q=0, and pVγ=constant\displaystyle pV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}pVγ=constant. So ΔU=−W\displaystyle \Delta U = -WΔU=−W: a gas that expands does work at the expense of its internal energy, and cools.

cards.q: For a gas heated at constant volume, how much work is done, and what happens to the energy supplied?
cards.a: No work is done, because the volume does not change. All the energy supplied increases the internal energy: Q=ΔU\displaystyle Q = \Delta UQ=ΔU.

cards.q: A gas at 1.0×105 Pa\displaystyle 1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}1.0×105 Pa is compressed adiabatically from 4.0×10−4 m3\displaystyle 4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}4.0×10−4 m3 to 1.0×10−4 m3\displaystyle 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}1.0×10−4 m3. Calculate its final pressure. (γ=1.4\displaystyle \gamma = 1.4γ=1.4)
cards.a: 7.0×105 Pa\displaystyle 7.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}7.0×105 Pa
cards.why: An isothermal compression to a quarter of the volume would give only four times the pressure: the adiabatic one also heats the gas.
steps: p1V1γ=p2V2γ\displaystyle p_{1}V_{1}^{\gamma} = p_{2}V_{2}^{\gamma}p1​V1γ​=p2​V2γ​, so p2=p1(V1V2)γ\displaystyle p_{2} = p_{1}\left(\frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}\right)^{\gamma}p2​=p1​(V2​V1​​)γ.
p2=1.0×105×4.01.4\displaystyle p_{2} = 1.0 \times 10^{5} \times 4.0^{1.4}p2​=1.0×105×4.01.4
4.01.4=6.96\displaystyle 4.0^{1.4} = 6.964.01.4=6.96, so p2=7.0×105 Pa\displaystyle p_{2} = 7.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}p2​=7.0×105 Pa

cards.q: On a p\displaystyle pp–V\displaystyle VV diagram, what does the area under a curve represent, and the area enclosed by a closed loop?
cards.a: The area under a curve is the work done in that process. The area of a closed loop is the net work done per cycle.

cards.q: On a p\displaystyle pp–V\displaystyle VV diagram, how does the curve for an adiabatic change compare with an isothermal curve through the same point?
cards.a: The adiabatic curve is steeper.
cards.why: In an adiabatic expansion the gas also cools, so its pressure falls faster than in an isothermal one.

cards.q: Name the four strokes of a four-stroke petrol engine, in order.
cards.a: Induction, compression, expansion (power) and exhaust.
cards.why: The fuel–air mixture is ignited by a spark at the end of the compression stroke.

cards.q: State two ways in which a diesel engine cycle differs from a petrol engine cycle.
cards.a: In a diesel engine only air is drawn in and compressed, to a much higher pressure and temperature. The fuel is injected at the end of compression and ignites without a spark, from the temperature of the air.

cards.q: Give two ways in which a real engine's indicator diagram differs from the theoretical diagram for its cycle.
cards.a: The corners are rounded, because valves take time to open and close and combustion is not instantaneous. The peak pressure is lower and the loop is smaller, and there is a small extra pumping loop for the induction and exhaust strokes.

cards.q: An engine burns fuel of calorific value 45 MJ kg−1\displaystyle 45\ \text{MJ kg}^{-1}45 MJ kg−1 at a rate of 2.0×10−3 kg s−1\displaystyle 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg s}^{-1}2.0×10−3 kg s−1. Calculate the input power.
cards.a: 9.0×104 W\displaystyle 9.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{W}9.0×104 W
steps: Input power = calorific value × fuel flow rate.
=45×106×2.0×10−3\displaystyle = 45 \times 10^{6} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3}=45×106×2.0×10−3
=9.0×104 W\displaystyle = 9.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{W}=9.0×104 W

cards.q: The p\displaystyle pp–V\displaystyle VV loop of one cylinder of an engine has an area of 500 J. The engine has 4 cylinders, each completing 25 cycles per second. Calculate the indicated power.
cards.a: 5.0×104 W\displaystyle 5.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{W}5.0×104 W
steps: Indicated power = area of loop × cycles per second × number of cylinders.
=500×25×4\displaystyle = 500 \times 25 \times 4=500×25×4
=5.0×104 W\displaystyle = 5.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{W}=5.0×104 W

cards.q: What are the brake power and the friction power of an engine?
cards.a: Brake power is the useful output power at the crankshaft: P=Tω\displaystyle P = T\omegaP=Tω. Friction power is the power lost to friction inside the engine: indicated power − brake power.

cards.q: Define the overall, thermal and mechanical efficiencies of an engine.
cards.a: Overall: brake powerinput power\displaystyle \frac{\text{brake power}}{\text{input power}}input powerbrake power​. Thermal: indicated powerinput power\displaystyle \frac{\text{indicated power}}{\text{input power}}input powerindicated power​. Mechanical: brake powerindicated power\displaystyle \frac{\text{brake power}}{\text{indicated power}}indicated powerbrake power​.
cards.why: Overall efficiency = thermal efficiency × mechanical efficiency.

cards.q: An engine has an input power of 90 kW, an indicated power of 50 kW and a brake power of 40 kW. Calculate its overall efficiency.
cards.a: 0.44 (44%)
cards.why: Its thermal efficiency is 0.56 and its mechanical efficiency 0.80.
steps: overall efficiency=brake powerinput power=4090\displaystyle \text{overall efficiency} = \frac{\text{brake power}}{\text{input power}} = \frac{40}{90}overall efficiency=input powerbrake power​=9040​
=0.44\displaystyle = 0.44=0.44

cards.q: What does the second law of thermodynamics say about a heat engine?
cards.a: A heat engine must operate between a hot source and a cold sink. It cannot turn all the energy it takes from the source into work: some must always be rejected to the sink.

cards.q: Write the efficiency of a heat engine in terms of the energy QH\displaystyle Q_{H}QH​ taken from the source and the energy QC\displaystyle Q_{C}QC​ rejected to the sink.
cards.a: efficiency=WQH=QH−QCQH\displaystyle \text{efficiency} = \frac{W}{Q_{H}} = \frac{Q_{H} - Q_{C}}{Q_{H}}efficiency=QH​W​=QH​QH​−QC​​

cards.q: A heat engine operates between a source at 750 K and a sink at 300 K. Calculate its maximum theoretical efficiency.
cards.a: 0.60 (60%)
steps: maximum efficiency=TH−TCTH\displaystyle \text{maximum efficiency} = \frac{T_{H} - T_{C}}{T_{H}}maximum efficiency=TH​TH​−TC​​, with temperatures in kelvin.
=750−300750\displaystyle = \frac{750 - 300}{750}=750750−300​
=0.60\displaystyle = 0.60=0.60

cards.q: Give three reasons why a real engine is less efficient than the theoretical maximum.
cards.a: Friction between moving parts, energy lost by heating the engine and its surroundings, and fuel that does not burn completely. The real processes are also not the ideal ones of the theoretical cycle.

cards.q: What is a combined heat and power scheme?
cards.a: A power station that uses the energy it would reject to the sink to heat nearby homes and buildings, as well as generating electricity. Much more of the energy from the fuel is put to use.

cards.q: What does a reversed heat engine do, and how do a refrigerator and a heat pump differ in purpose?
cards.a: Work is done on it to transfer energy from a cold space to a hot space. A refrigerator is used to remove energy from the cold space; a heat pump is used to deliver energy to the hot space.

cards.q: Write the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator and of a heat pump.
cards.a: Refrigerator: COPref=QCW=QCQH−QC\displaystyle COP_{\text{ref}} = \frac{Q_{C}}{W} = \frac{Q_{C}}{Q_{H} - Q_{C}}COPref​=WQC​​=QH​−QC​QC​​. Heat pump: COPhp=QHW=QHQH−QC\displaystyle COP_{\text{hp}} = \frac{Q_{H}}{W} = \frac{Q_{H}}{Q_{H} - Q_{C}}COPhp​=WQH​​=QH​−QC​QH​​.
cards.why: Each is the energy you want, divided by the work you pay for. The heat pump's is always 1 more than the refrigerator's.

cards.q: An ideal refrigerator keeps its inside at 270 K in a room at 300 K. Calculate its maximum coefficient of performance.
cards.a: 9.0
cards.why: A coefficient of performance is usually greater than 1: it is not an efficiency.
steps: COPref=TCTH−TC\displaystyle COP_{\text{ref}} = \frac{T_{C}}{T_{H} - T_{C}}COPref​=TH​−TC​TC​​
=270300−270\displaystyle = \frac{270}{300 - 270}=300−270270​
=9.0\displaystyle = 9.0=9.0

cards.q: A heat pump uses 1.0 kW of electrical power and delivers 3.5 kW of heating to a house. Calculate its coefficient of performance.
cards.a: 3.5
steps: COPhp=QHW=3.51.0\displaystyle COP_{\text{hp}} = \frac{Q_{H}}{W} = \frac{3.5}{1.0}COPhp​=WQH​​=1.03.5​
=3.5\displaystyle = 3.5=3.5
